comment: How does no one here including Mr Munj know that every single car or motorcycle comes from the factory with the speedometer calibrated to read 5 to 10% above the actual GPS or radar speed? This is done for liability reasons so manufacturers don't get sued when someone gets busted for speeding while the speedometer showed the driver was under the speed limit. A 5% difference is exactly what you'd expect, so it's not an error. I had a Benelli motorcycle that had a 10% offset, which was extremely annoying as it showed you traveling much faster than you actually were. If you fit bigger wheels on your vehicle the speed offset will reduce and likely begin under-reporting the speed the faster you go.

comment: Here is some good advice for driving an automatic car.
title: GWM P500 takes on different test drive challenges! 🚙⚡

comment: Mistake # 1 Driving too close to the car 🚗 in front and braking too late Maintaining a safe following distance is fundamental, but many drivers end up driving too close to the car in front of them and braking too late. In automatic cars, it's even worse because the transmission can mask the sensation of speed. The key is to observe the road and release the accelerator before you need to brake. This not only improves safety but also saves fuel and reduces brake wear. Braking smoothly is always the best solution. Now that you know these common mistakes, you can avoid problems and extend the life of your automatic car. Small changes in driving habits can make all the difference, helping you save money and keep your vehicle in good condition.
title: GWM P500 takes on different test drive challenges! 🚙⚡

comment: Mistake # 2 Shifting gears by skipping steps In automatic cars, the transmission shifts gears automatically, but sometimes you need to manually shift to R, N, or L. The problem is that some drivers do this abruptly or skip gears, which can wear out the system. Rapid and erratic gear changes can damage the internal components of the gearbox. Always follow the correct shift order and avoid forcing the gear lever. Your gearbox is designed to operate smoothly, so let it do its job properly.
title: GWM P500 takes on different test drive challenges! 🚙⚡

comment: Mistake # 3 ignore the warning lights on the dashboard If one in ten drivers ignores warning lights until it's too late, yet these lights are there to signal problems before they worsen, red lights indicate serious faults such as engine overheating, insufficient oil pressure, or braking problems. Yellow or amber lights are warnings to heed, such as low tire pressure or the need for an engine service. If any of these lights come on, stop the car in a safe place and consult the owner's manual to understand the problem. Small warnings can prevent big losses.
title: GWM P500 takes on different test drive challenges! 🚙⚡

comment: Mistake #4 Putting the car 🚗 in Park without engaging the handbrake Many people think that the automatic transmission's Park mode alone holds the car 🚗, but it's not as effective as the parking brake when parking on a slope or uneven ground. The car's weight 🚗 rests on the transmission, causing wear over time ⏲️. This stress can lead to the locking mechanism failing, causing the car 🚗 to roll away. The parking brake relieves this pressure, preventing damage to the transmission and accidents, even on level ground. It's a good habit to use it; it may seem like a small detail, but ignoring it can lead to costly repairs in the future.
title: GWM P500 takes on different test drive challenges! 🚙⚡

comment: Mistake 5 ) Driving in Deep Water 💧 Many people think they can drive through a flooded area without any problems, but this is a mistake that can be very costly if you don't understand how a gearbox works. Gearboxes are equipped with decompression vents that can eventually let water in. On 4x4 vehicles, these vents are located higher, which reduces the risk, but on conventional models, they are much lower, making water infiltration a serious problem. When water mixes with the transmission fluid, it forms a milky substance that destroys the clutch discs, and the worst part is that this can happen in just a few hours. Simply draining the fluid is useless because the damage is already done; in most cases, the transmission must be completely replaced. In other words, if your car isn't ready for off-roading, avoid deep water at all costs.
title: GWM P500 takes on different test drive challenges! 🚙⚡

comment: Mistake 6 ) Place your hand on the gear lever This may seem like a harmless habit, but resting your hand on the gear lever can cause damage over time. This constant pressure puts stress on the gear shift fork and the transmission synchronizers, making gear changes less smooth. If the pressure is too high, it can accelerate wear on the synchronizer ring in the Leon, which impairs the gear lever's performance. To better understand, think of a brick on the grass; over time, it leaves a mark. The same applies to transmission components. Over the years, some more modern cars use wire cables instead of direct mechanical links, which helps reduce the impact of vibrations. However, this doesn't mean the problem disappears. Ideally, keep both hands on the steering wheel and avoid resting your hand on the gear lever.
title: GWM P500 takes on different test drive challenges! 🚙⚡

comment: Mistake 7 ) turning the engine on and off too often Switching off the engine occasionally isn't a problem, but doing so frequently can accelerate wear on the starter and battery. The starter and battery are under more strain with each start, and this increased wear can negatively impact the vehicle's overall performance. If you're stopped briefly, such as at a red light, leaving the engine running is fine. However, if the stop lasts several minutes, switching it off saves fuel and reduces wear. Many modern cars are equipped with automatic start-stop systems that shut off the engine when the vehicle comes to a stop. This demonstrates that occasional stops aren't harmful, but frequent manual stops can overload the battery and ignition components.
title: GWM P500 takes on different test drive challenges! 🚙⚡

comment: Mistake 8 ) Turn off the engine immediately after intensive driving. If you drive a manual car, you naturally downshift when you decelerate, allowing the engine to cool down gradually. However, in automatic vehicles, the engine continues to operate at a higher temperature even after being switched off. Turning off the car immediately after a demanding drive can interrupt the flow of oil and coolant, leading to a buildup of internal heat known as thermal overload. This can accelerate wear on components and, on older vehicles, increase the risk of cracks in the exhaust manifolds. If your car is turbocharged, this precaution is even more crucial. Turbos spin at very high speeds (over 100,000 RPM) and rely on constant lubrication. Switching off the engine prematurely can interrupt the oil flow and cause long-term damage. Ideally, wait at least a minute or two before switching off the engine after spirited driving.
title: GWM P500 takes on different test drive challenges! 🚙⚡

comment: Mistake 9 ) Leave the car 🚗 idling for too long Although it doesn't cause immediate engine damage, leaving the car 🚗 idling for extended periods leads to unnecessary wear. Even when stopped, the engine continues to run, activating components such as the alternator and belts. Over time, this contributes to vehicle wear without adding any mileage. You may have heard that highway driving puts less strain on the engine than city driving. Indeed, in urban traffic, idling periods and frequent stops are more common. Furthermore, leaving the engine running unnecessarily reduces fuel efficiency. Incomplete combustion can generate carbon deposits that foul spark plugs and increase fuel consumption. Unburned fuel can also mix with the engine oil, compromising its efficiency and requiring more frequent oil changes. If you have to wait a long time, the best solution is to leave the car in Park (P) or simply turn off the engine.
title: GWM P500 takes on different test drive challenges! 🚙⚡

comment: Mistake #10: Leaving the car in neutral on downhill slopes Many drivers think that putting the car in neutral on downhill slopes saves fuel, but this isn't true in modern vehicles. The engine automatically reduces fuel consumption when the car decelerates in gear. Furthermore, in some countries, this practice is illegal. Besides not saving fuel, leaving the car in neutral jeopardizes your safety. In this position, you lose control of acceleration and risk not being able to react quickly in an emergency. Ideally, you should downshift manually to maintain control and ensure a safe descent.
title: GWM P500 takes on different test drive challenges! 🚙⚡

comment: MISTAKE #12 TURN OFF the car before parking. Always the Keep your foot on the brake when you shift the gear lever into Park (P) and engage the parking brake before releasing the pedal. This is a simple but essential habit to avoid problems. Most modern cars are equipped with systems that prevent the engine from shutting off when the vehicle is not properly parked. However, if your car is not equipped with this feature, you are taking a risk. If the vehicle is not fully parked, it can move on its own, especially if the parking brake is not engaged. In neutral, the car can slide in any direction, increasing the risk of an accident. Furthermore, improper stopping can damage the transmission system

comment: Mistake #13: ACCELERATION When the Engine is Cold. When the engine is still cold, parts such as pistons and rings are not fully expanded. This can lead to premature wear. Furthermore, the lubricating oil 🛢 hasn't yet circulated properly because 🚗 when cold, it thickens and takes longer to flow, making it difficult to lubricate internal parts. Accelerating immediately after starting forces the engine to work without Optimal lubrication increases wear and reduces engine life. To avoid this problem, wait for the engine to warm up before driving aggressively. In warm weather, one minute of idling is sufficient; in cold weather, wait 5 minutes. Do not rely solely on the coolant temperature gauge, as oil takes longer to reach its ideal temperature. Even if the dashboard indicates the engine is warm, it may not yet be ready for sudden acceleration.

comment: Mistake #14: Unnecessary Modifications Making modifications to your car 🚗 might seem like a good idea to improve performance, but it often ends up compromising reliability, increasing fuel consumption, and even voiding the warranty. If you're looking for increased performance, it's better to invest in a module designed for that purpose rather than spending money 💰 on upgrades that could cause problems in the future.

If this part fails, the car 🚗 can move on its own, which can lead to dangerous situations. Another common mistake is shifting from Drive (D) to Reverse (R) without coming to a complete stop. This overloads the transmission, which can lead to repairs costing 3,000 Rupees on some models. I checked it out on PAPS and this CBU unit has quality issues, imagine what will happen to local made , the material used in seats seems like recycled fibres, (imagine an AC airfilter texture) plastics are pretty scratchy feeling as well. Size wise it will compete with Suzuki's Swift and it seems in the same segment as well. Although to compete with Swift KIA has to open its parts market to third tier suppliers, KIA is still protecting its dealerships where the car owner isnt even allowed to be in the shop to observe what they are doing to their car. Parts and service are exorbitantly high and having no resale plus the burden of a previous failed model on the new stonic. KIA needs to be really careful how they price it. The only thing they have going for stonic is its lifetime token, FBR concession and shape to match its expensive variants. Sadly from history we know KIA will price it 6 mill + , elantra Special Edition /Altis X and used Grande will eat it alive. Suzuki will still have a success with their swift and in 3 years KIA will discontinue stonic. Those 300 poor souls that wanted CITY SUV will have a dud on their hands with no resale and no parts.

comment: 13:40 no battery tech allows you to drain to true 0% without destroying its longevity. The 20-80% rule is just standard user advice for daily driving, but the hardware buffer is different. When brands sell an EV with 100% usable DoD, it’s a BMS-controlled limit, not a raw hardware limit. If the physical pack is 66kWh, they might restrict usable energy to 60kWh. When your screen shows 0%, you are at the bottom of that 60kWh limit, while the remaining 6kWh is locked away as a safety buffer so the car doesn't brick itself. btw the following text is from GAC Avoid charging the battery to 100% every day: ideally, keep the charge level between 20% and 80% during daily use. comment: You've given a very fair and authentic review. I'm also driving the Jaecoo J7 and have covered over 4,000 km so far. Around 2,500–3,000 km of that has been in EV mode, and I can honestly say it's a very good car. The maximum I've driven in EV mode is 105 km on the highway, but I had it set to EV+ mode. Its Super Hybrid System is excellent. The issues mentioned in the video are the same ones I'm experiencing. The front driver's side door sometimes requires a little extra force to close, and I also hear a noise from the moonroof when driving over speed breakers. The underbody protective sheet is currently unavailable, but I've been told it should arrive by the end of July or in August. I'll have it installed during the 5,000 km service. The company has assured me that they'll fix all these issues when I bring the car in. Other than that, I'm very satisfied with the car. It's an excellent vehicle, MashaAllah.
